content: Radioactive dentin abrasion is a procedure designed to measure the abrasion of either tooth enamel or dentin using human teeth that have been rendered radioactive through mild neutron irradiation. The term abrasive refers to a cleaning agent in dentifrices (toothpastes) that, in combination with the mechanical action of a toothbrush, removes food particles and dental plaque from the teeth. Various abrasives are commonly incorporated into commercial toothpastes, including dicalcium phosphate, hydrated silica, and sodium bicarbonate (commonly known as baking soda). The radioactive dentin abrasion method for assessing the abrasiveness of dentifrices on human teeth was first described in 1958 by researchers R.J. Grabenstetter, R.W. Broge, F.L. Jackson, and A.W. Radike in their publication titled The Measurement of the Abrasion of Human Teeth by Dentifrice Abrasives: A Test Utilizing Radioactive Teeth. This method is more precise and efficient compared to earlier techniques, which relied on measuring the depth of grooves cut into tooth structures. The earlier methods, first studied by W.D. Miller in 1907, were less accurate and more time-consuming. In contrast, the radioactive dentin abrasion method directly quantifies the amount of human tooth structure worn away by a toothbrush and a dentifrice abrasive slurry under controlled conditions, including constant brush pressure and stroke speed. The test demonstrates a coefficient of variation of 6-7 when eight replicates are performed, and 10-15 when only duplicates are conducted, as is typical in routine testing. This represents a significant improvement, with variability reduced to one-half to one-fourth of that observed in the depth-of-cut method. Additionally, results can be obtained in one-half to one-third of the time required by the older technique.
